Sample text:
---
# On Blue

Blue is strange. Among the colors we see easily, it is the one nature offers least. Ripe fruit is red, orange, or yellow. Leaves are green. Blood, flowers, and sunsets run warm. Blue is rare on the surface of living things, so much so that many languages were slow to name it. Some ancient texts describe the sea as wine-dark and never mention a blue sea at all.

Most of the blue we see is not pigment. A jay's feathers contain no blue dye. Their structure is built from tiny layers of keratin and air that scatter short wavelengths back to the eye, the same physics that makes the sky look blue. Blue is often an illusion made of light bending on nanoscale architecture. A blue morpho butterfly's wing, under a microscope, looks like a set of tiny staircases that catch the light just so. Nature can make blue, but it usually prefers to do it with tricks.

Humans had to work harder. For centuries the finest blue came from lapis lazuli, a stone mined mainly in the mountains of Afghanistan and shipped across continents. Grinding it into ultramarine was laborious, and the pigment was costly enough that Renaissance painters sometimes wrote into their contracts exactly how much they would use, and who would pay for it. The Virgin's robes in many famous altarpieces are wrapped in that expensive blue, a signal of devotion made visible through cost. A color became a kind of currency.

Then, in the 1800s, chemists learned to make synthetic ultramarine, and the price fell dramatically. Blue jeans, which began as sturdy workwear dyed with indigo, became ordinary in a way that would have baffled a fifteenth-century painter. Something that once required a trade route and a fortune now sits on half the people you pass on the street.

I find something moving in that arc: the color that was rarest in nature became, for a while, the most precious thing a human could buy, and then the most common thing a human could wear. Our relationship to beauty is shaped by scarcity and cost, and when the cost disappears, we often stop noticing the beauty altogether. I suspect most people who wear blue every day could not say when they last really looked at it.

So here is a small suggestion: the next time you see blue, the sky in a window, a stranger's coat, the hour just after sunset when the light goes cool, stop for a second. You are looking at light that has been scattered, bent, and filtered on its way to you, and the fact that it reaches you at all, in a world that mostly favors warmer colors, is a small accident worth noticing.
---
